analysis.one_liner: Cancels federal oil and gas leases held by companies that team up with OPEC to manipulate oil prices.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2024, referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: If the Federal Trade Commission issued a final order finding that a company holding a federal oil or gas lease coordinated with an OPEC or OPEC-plus country to manipulate prices in violation of antitrust law, the Interior Secretary would have to cancel that company's federal leases, never renew or extend them, and bar it from bidding on future federal leases. The bill never moved past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and taxpayers. Federal leases are a public resource; the bill would strip that privilege from companies a final FTC order found were coordinating with foreign cartels to push prices up. Motorists, homeowners with heating bills, and any business exposed to energy costs would benefit if it deterred price coordination.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers paying gasoline and heating bills

how_it_helps.text: Under the bill, once the FTC issues a final order finding a leaseholder coordinated with an OPEC or OPEC-plus country to manipulate oil or gas prices in violation of the Sherman or Clayton Act, the Interior Secretary must cancel that holder's federal leases and can never renew or extend them.
The bill also permanently bans such a company from bidding on any new federal oil and gas lease starting the day the FTC order issues.
The bill names 11 OPEC countries and 10 OPEC-plus countries — including Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iran, Venezuela, and Mexico — as the cartel partners that would trigger lease cancellation.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that lose federal leases and bidding rights after a final FTC price-manipulation order, and possibly federal royalty revenue from canceled leases. Companies would also face the risk of losing access to publicly owned oil and gas if they coordinated with foreign cartels.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies with FTC findings

drawbacks.text: Enforcement depends entirely on the FTC first winning a final antitrust order proving coordination with an OPEC country — a high legal bar that the bill does nothing to lower, so it may rarely apply in practice.

Canceling federal leases and barring bidders could reduce federal royalty income and domestic production from disciplined companies, and opponents would argue it politicizes federal leasing by attaching antitrust penalties to an administrative resource program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's practical reach is narrow: it only triggers after the FTC wins a final order against a company for coordinating with a named cartel country, which is rare. But as a deterrent and penalty it directly ties access to public oil resources to honest pricing conduct, and its costs fall on the small set of companies that would meet that bar.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Natural Resources Committee with no markup, vote, or floor action before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 24, 2024, less than six months before the end of the two-year Congress.
It was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the day it was introduced and received no further action.
No committee vote, no floor vote, and no Senate action ever occurred; the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies keep their federal leases and full access to public oil and gas resources with no added penalty for price coordination with foreign cartels.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies with federal leases

for.name: Nanette Barragán
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 13 Democratic cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and it stayed in committee with no floor action.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies holding federal leases
industries.note: Any company found by a final FTC order to have coordinated with an OPEC or OPEC-plus country to manipulate prices would lose its federal leases and be barred from future bidding. Companies with clean antitrust records would face no direct penalty.
